prompt: In a cluster of three nodes, what decides which node stores a partition?

choices.text: The token its partition key hashes to, and who owns that range
choices.why: Right. Murmur3 turns the key into a token and the ring says who owns that point.

choices.text: The node the client happened to be connected to when it wrote the row
choices.why: That node is only the coordinator; it forwards the write to the owners.

choices.text: The alphabetical order of the keys, split evenly between the nodes
choices.why: The rows came back in token order, carla before bruno before ana; the hash scatters neighbours.

choices.text: The node with the most free disk at the moment of the write
choices.why: Placement is a function of the key alone, so any node can compute it without asking.

prompt: `nodetool ring` lists a node's token as `8538878424377726911` and the token on the line above as `8141555572029014120`. Which partition keys does that node own?
hint: A node owns the range that ends at its token.

choices.text: Those whose token is above 8141555572029014120 and up to 8538878424377726911
choices.why: Right. Ana's token, 8413089589345688709, is in that range, which is why she is on that node.

choices.text: Those whose token starts at 8538878424377726911 and runs to the next line
choices.why: That is the next node's range: ownership ends at a token, it does not start there.

choices.text: Only the key whose token is exactly 8538878424377726911
choices.why: A token marks the end of a whole range of keys, not one key.

choices.text: Every key, since the token only says where its first copy goes
choices.why: With one copy per partition, each key has exactly one owner.

prompt: The lab's three nodes each own 16 tokens. How many lines with `Normal` does `nodetool ring` print for the cluster?
A fourth node joins a cluster where each node owns 16 small ranges spread round the ring. Compared with one big range per node, what changes?
hint: Think of where the new node's ranges come from.

choices.text: It takes small pieces from every existing node, so the load evens out
choices.why: Right. With one range per node it would split one neighbour's range and leave the others as they were.

choices.text: It has to wait until the others have moved every partition to rebalance alphabetically
choices.why: Keys are placed by token, never alphabetically.

choices.text: Nothing, because tokens are only an index and do not decide placement
choices.why: Tokens are the placement; getendpoints computes the node from them.

choices.text: It halves one neighbour's range, which is why 16 tokens are slower to add
choices.why: That is what happens with one token per node, the case 16 avoids.

prompt: Why does the lesson's loop wait for each node to be `UN` before starting the next one?

choices.text: Because `docker run` refuses to start two containers from the same image at once
choices.why: Docker has no such rule; the waiting is for Cassandra.

choices.text: A joining node takes its share of the ring from the others, one join at a time
choices.why: Right. Cassandra expects joins one after another.

choices.text: Because c2 and c3 need c1's data copied in before they can start
choices.why: There is no data yet when the cluster is built; it is the ring that is shared out.

choices.text: Because each container needs the whole 4 GB while it is starting
choices.why: With the small heap each node uses about 500 MB, and the loop is about joining, not memory.

prompt: `orders_by_customer` is created `WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (ordered_at DESC, order_id ASC)`. What does `SELECT ... WHERE customer = 'ana@example.com' LIMIT 1` return?

choices.text: Ana's most recent order, read as the first row of her partition
choices.why: Right: A-1006, from 8 April. The stored order is newest first.

choices.text: The first order Ana ever placed
choices.why: That would be the answer with ASC; DESC puts the newest on top.

choices.text: Any one of Ana's orders, since rows have no order without ORDER BY
choices.why: Inside a partition the rows have the clustering order, on disk.

choices.text: An error, because LIMIT needs an ORDER BY
choices.why: LIMIT works alone and takes rows in the stored order.

prompt: A table is `PRIMARY KEY (customer, ordered_at)`. A customer places two orders in the same millisecond, and both inserts succeed. What is in the table afterwards?
hint: What does an INSERT do with a key that exists?

choices.text: Two rows, because each INSERT adds a row
choices.why: An INSERT with an existing primary key replaces that row.

choices.text: One row, holding the second order, with no error raised
choices.why: Right. That is why the lesson adds order_id as a last clustering column.

choices.text: One row, and the second INSERT fails with a duplicate key error
choices.why: Cassandra does not check before writing; both inserts succeed.

choices.text: Two rows in different partitions, one per order
choices.why: The partition key is the customer, the same for both.

prompt: Match each part of `PRIMARY KEY (customer, ordered_at, order_id)` to what it decides.

pairs.right: the order of rows inside the partition, and the ranges you can ask for
what keeps two orders at the same instant apart

prompt: Which `ORDER BY` does Cassandra refuse on `orders_by_customer`, with the partition named?

choices.text: ORDER BY ordered_at ASC
choices.why: Reversing the clustering order is allowed: it reads the partition backwards.

choices.text: ORDER BY total DESC
choices.why: Right: total is not a clustering column, and only those can be ordered by.

choices.text: ORDER BY ordered_at DESC
choices.why: That is the stored order itself.

choices.text: ORDER BY ordered_at DESC, order_id ASC
choices.why: That repeats the table's clustering order exactly.

prompt: A query with `ALLOW FILTERING` returned the right three orders in milliseconds on the lab. Why is it still a bad choice for the application's main screen?

choices.text: Because its results are not guaranteed to be correct
choices.why: The answer was correct; the refusal is about cost.

choices.text: Its cost grows with the size of the table, not of the answer
choices.why: Right. It sent range requests over all 49 ranges; with eighty million rows each request scans its share.

choices.text: Because ALLOW FILTERING is removed in Cassandra 5.0 and will stop working
choices.why: It ran on 5.0.9 in the lab.

choices.text: Because it only reads the coordinator's own data and misses the rest
choices.why: The trace shows it asking c2 and c3 as well.

prompt: After `CREATE INDEX ... USING 'sai'` on `status`, the trace of `WHERE status = 'shipped'` still shows `Submitting range requests on 49 ranges`. What does that tell you?
hint: Where does a secondary index live?

choices.text: The index was not used, and the query fell back to filtering
choices.why: It was used: no ALLOW FILTERING was needed, and each node read only the matching partitions.

choices.text: The index is still being built, and a second run will go to one node
choices.why: A finished SAI index still has to be asked on every node.

choices.text: Each node indexes only its own data, so every node still has to be asked
choices.why: Right. SAI makes each node's part cheaper; it cannot point the coordinator at one node.

choices.text: The coordinator always splits every query into 49 ranges, indexed or not
choices.why: A query naming the partition key was one single-partition read, with no ranges.

prompt: Put the lesson's method for designing a Cassandra table in order.
items: Write down the query the screen will run, with its parameters
Make the parameter always given with = the partition key
Make what the query sorts or ranges on the clustering columns
Add what makes a row unique as the last clustering column
Check that the partition cannot grow without bound
trap: The query comes first; the table is its answer.

prompt: The warehouse needs "every order placed on a given day". What does the lesson do?

choices.text: Adds an SAI index on ordered_at to orders_by_customer
choices.why: Every node would still be asked, for the warehouse's main query.

choices.text: Creates orders_by_day, partitioned by day, and writes each order to both tables
choices.why: Right. One table per query, and the day's orders are one partition.

choices.text: Runs the existing query with ALLOW FILTERING on a range of ordered_at
choices.why: That reads every partition on every node to answer a one-day question.

choices.text: Changes orders_by_customer's partition key to the day
choices.why: Then the account page's query would break; each question keeps its own table.

prompt: A query on a column outside the primary key is refused unless it ends with ALLOW ___.
In `PRIMARY KEY ((customer, month), viewed_at)`, what do the inner parentheses do?

choices.text: They make customer and month together the partition key
choices.why: Right: one partition per customer per month.

choices.text: They make month a clustering column sorted before viewed_at
choices.why: Without the inner parentheses month would be a clustering column; with them it is part of the partition key.

choices.text: They are an optional grouping, with no effect at all on how rows are stored
choices.why: They change where every row lives.

choices.text: They create a secondary index on month
choices.why: Indexes are made with CREATE INDEX, never by the key's parentheses.

prompt: Ana's unbucketed partition reached about 1.1 MB in 90 days of a view every five minutes. At the same rate, about how many MB will it hold after 10 years (3650 days)?
A sensor writes a reading every second into `readings (sensor, at)` with `sensor` as the partition key. Which change does the lesson's reasoning point to?

choices.text: Add a day or an hour to the partition key, so each partition stops growing
choices.why: Right. The rate decides the bucket; a second-by-second sensor needs a small one.

choices.text: Add an SAI index on at, so reads of recent readings stay fast
choices.why: An index does not shrink the partition; it keeps growing on the same nodes.

choices.text: Raise the number of tokens per node so the partition is split across nodes
choices.why: A partition is never split: it lives whole on the owners of its token.

choices.text: Nothing, since a partition only becomes a problem above 100 MB
choices.why: At one write a second that partition passes the guidance within weeks, and never stops.

prompt: In the lab's `tablestats`, which node held `views_by_customer`'s one partition, and what did the other two hold of it?

choices.text: c2 held all of it; c1 and c3 held nothing of that table
choices.why: Right. With one copy and one partition, one node carries Ana's whole history.

choices.text: Each node held a third of it, split by month
choices.why: That was the bucketed table, whose key includes the month.

choices.text: c1 held it, because c1 coordinated the COPY
choices.why: The coordinator forwards rows to the owners of their token.

choices.text: All three held a full copy, as replicas
choices.why: The keyspace has one copy in this lesson; lesson 17 raises it.

prompt: What does bucketing cost the application?

choices.text: Every write becomes slower, since the month must be computed by Cassandra
choices.why: The application supplies the month; the write is the same size.

choices.text: A query for recent rows names a month, and asks for the one before when it needs more
choices.why: Right: a loop in the application instead of one query.

choices.text: Old months can no longer be read once their bucket closes
choices.why: A closed bucket is still a partition you can read; it just stops growing.

choices.text: The data takes three times the disk space
choices.why: The same rows are stored once, split into smaller partitions.

prompt: Which of these queries go to one partition on `orders_by_customer`, `orders_by_day` and the tables of this lesson? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Ana's orders in March, from orders_by_customer
choices.why: Right: customer named, range on the first clustering column.

choices.text: Every shipped order, through the SAI index
choices.why: SAI still asks every node.

choices.text: The orders of 2 March, from orders_by_day
choices.why: Right: the day is the partition key.

choices.text: Ana's views in February, from views_by_customer_month
choices.why: Right: customer and month together name the partition.

choices.text: Every order above 1000, with ALLOW FILTERING
choices.why: It reads all 49 ranges.

prompt: A colleague proposes `PRIMARY KEY (status, ordered_at)` for a table of orders, so the shop can list orders by status. What does this lesson predict?
hint: How many different values does status have?

choices.text: A few partitions, one per status, that grow forever on a few nodes
choices.why: Right. Three statuses means three partitions holding every order the shop ever takes.

choices.text: An even spread over the nodes, since the hash scatters any key it is given
choices.why: The hash spreads different keys; with three values there are three partitions to spread.

choices.text: A refusal at CREATE TABLE time, because status is not unique per order
choices.why: A partition key need not be unique; uniqueness comes from the whole primary key.

choices.text: The same result as an SAI index on status
choices.why: SAI spreads the rows by their real key and asks every node; this piles them into three partitions.
